question: Elbow position in bench press
answer:
For bench press elbow position, use this setup:

• Keep elbows about 45 to 75 degrees from your torso (not fully flared at 90)
• Wrists stacked over elbows at the bottom position
• Forearms mostly vertical when the bar touches lower chest/sternum area
• Tuck slightly on the way down, then press up and slightly back
• Keep shoulder blades retracted and down to protect shoulders

Common mistakes:
• Elbows too wide (shoulder stress)
• Elbows too tucked (triceps-dominant, unstable bar path)
• Bouncing bar off chest

Cue: 'Stack wrist-elbow, touch low chest, press back toward eyes.'

question: Squat depth requirements
answer:
For squat depth, use this practical standard:

• General goal: descend until hip crease is at or slightly below top of knee
• Keep full-foot pressure (big toe, little toe, heel) to avoid collapsing forward
• Knees track over toes; avoid cave-in
• Maintain neutral spine and brace before each rep
• Depth should be pain-free and controlled with stable bar path

If you cannot hit depth yet, improve these first:
• Ankle dorsiflexion mobility
• Hip external rotation control
• Core bracing and tempo (3-second eccentric)

Useful progression: goblet squat to box, then gradually lower box height.

question: Signs you need a deload
answer:
Common signs you likely need a deload:

• Performance stalls or drops for 2+ weeks
• Usual weights feel unusually heavy (high RPE)
• Persistent joint/tendon soreness
• Poor sleep, low motivation, irritability
• Elevated resting heart rate and poor recovery between sessions

Deload approach (7 days):
• Reduce load to ~60-70% or cut volume by 40-50%
• Keep movement patterns but avoid failure
• Prioritize sleep, hydration, and steps

question: Metabolic adaptation to dieting
answer:
Metabolic adaptation is your body's response to prolonged calorie deficit:

• Resting energy expenditure can drop
• Non-exercise activity often decreases subconsciously
• Hunger can increase while satiety drops
• Training output may decline over time

How to manage it:
• Use moderate deficits, not aggressive crashes
• Keep protein high and resistance training consistent
• Include diet breaks/refeed periods when needed
• Sleep 7-9 hours and manage stress
• Transition out with reverse dieting after long cuts

key: diet::coming out of a diet without gaining fat
question: Coming out of a diet without gaining fat
answer:
To come out of a diet without rapid fat gain, use a reverse-diet transition:

• Increase calories gradually (about 80-150 kcal/week)
• Keep protein high (~1.6-2.2 g/kg body weight)
• Add carbs first to support training and recovery
• Hold body weight gain to ~0.1-0.25% per week
• Keep lifting performance trending up
• Keep daily steps/cardio stable for 2-3 weeks before reducing

Use waist + scale trend + gym performance to adjust each week.

key: fitness::how to engage lats in pull-ups
question: How to engage lats in pull-ups
answer:
To engage lats better in pull-ups, use these cues:

• Start from an active hang: depress shoulders (pull shoulder blades down) before bending elbows
• Think 'drive elbows to your back pockets' instead of pulling with hands
• Keep ribs down and slight hollow-body tension to avoid swinging
• Use a shoulder-width or just-wider grip; very wide grips often reduce quality ROM
• Pause 1 second at the top and lower with control for 2-3 seconds

Drills to improve lat activation:
• Scap pull-ups (2-3 sets of 8-12)
• Straight-arm pulldowns
• Chest-supported rows with elbow path close to torso

• Avoid screens 30 minutes before bed

key: health::why does my back hurt after deadlifts?
question: why does my back hurt after deadlifts?
answer:
Back pain after deadlifts usually comes from setup or load management issues:

• Keep a neutral spine and brace hard before each rep
• Keep the bar close to your shins and thighs throughout
• Avoid jerking the bar off the floor
• Reduce load 10-20% and rebuild with strict technique
• Add core stability and hip hinge drills between sessions

Stop and seek professional evaluation if pain is sharp, radiates down the leg, or persists beyond a few days.

question: what is progressive overload
answer:
Progressive overload is how you keep improving over time:

• Add a little weight, reps, or sets when performance is stable
• Keep form strict so the stress stays on the target muscles
• Use small jumps, especially on upper-body lifts
• Deload every few weeks if fatigue is building

Core principle: Gradually increase weight, reps, or intensity to continue seeing results
Recovery principle: Rest is when muscles grow and repair; ensure 7-9 hours sleep
Form principle: Perfect form with lighter weight beats poor form with heavy weight
